video_title: Lawfare Daily: Breaking Down Trump’s Diesel Deal with Russia
gist: Lawfare panel (Rachel Alpert, Peter Harrell) dissects Trump's Russian diesel deal and OFAC General License 135: legally contested under the 2022 import ban, unlikely to attract US importers, and too small to move diesel prices, with Ukraine refinery strikes and the Oct 18 Graham tariff provision as the real variables.

insights.claim: OFAC General License 135 authorizes transactions for the sale, delivery, offloading and importation (including into the US) of Russian-origin diesel until April 7, 2027, overriding prohibitions under EO 14066 and both the Russia Harmful Foreign Activities and Ukraine-Russia sanctions programs.
insights.speaker: Rachel Alpert
insights.so_what: Defines the legal window and scope for any Russian diesel trade; the April 2027 expiry is the key date to watch.

insights.claim: GL 135 covers future-produced Russian diesel, unlike GL 133/134/134B issued in April-May, which applied only to product already on the water, implying the administration expects a longer-duration arrangement.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
insights.so_what: Signals a structural rather than a stopgap easing of Russian energy sanctions.

insights.claim: GL 135 is a revocable authorization, not an actual lifting of sanctions, and companies have seen general licenses pulled quickly (the Iran general license is cited as the recent example), so counterparties may hesitate to rely on it.
insights.speaker: Rachel Alpert
insights.so_what: Revocation risk caps the volume of real-money participation in Russian diesel.

insights.claim: The license only lifts US sanctions; EU and UK sanctions still apply and nothing was coordinated with allies, so shipping, brokering and insurance for Russian diesel remain constrained for any firm with non-US touchpoints.
insights.speaker: Rachel Alpert
insights.so_what: Limits the supply-side effect and complicates vessels, insurers and flagging for any transaction.

insights.claim: The 2022 Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act bans imports of all HTS Chapter 27 products and sets a congressional review process with certification criteria (essentially peace with Ukraine) for lifting the ban, which creates a statutory barrier separate from the IEEPA sanctions that GL 135 licenses.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
entities: Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act
insights.so_what: Whether a license can override a statute is the crux of the legality question for US diesel imports.

insights.claim: The administration's best statutory argument rests on the Act's phrase that the ban be implemented 'in a manner consistent with any implementation actions issued under Executive Order 14066,' which could encompass OFAC licensing, supported by legislative history in which a stronger notwithstanding clause and waiver mechanism were dropped.
insights.speaker: Rachel Alpert
entities: Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act
insights.so_what: Likely the reading OFAC counsel relies on; an ambiguous statute means any court outcome is uncertain.
insights.quote: in a manner consistent with any implementation actions issued under Executive Order 14066

insights.claim: Harrell argues Congress intended only to ratify the then-existing wind-down license (about three more weeks of imports), because an open-ended licensing power would make the Act's elaborate termination criteria and congressional review meaningless.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
entities: Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act
insights.so_what: Supports the view that the import authorization is unlawful and legally risky for importers.

insights.claim: Post-Loper Bright, courts give agencies less deference on statutory interpretation, which adds risk to the executive branch's reading of the import ban, though how far that applies in national security is unclear.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
insights.so_what: Raises litigation risk for the license if it is ever challenged.

insights.claim: Harrell suspects the president decided the policy on his call with Putin and lawyers then squared the legal circles after the fact, rather than OFAC counsel vetting it beforehand.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
insights.so_what: Suggests thin legal groundwork and policy volatility; Alpert agreed this was likely.

themes.theme: Why US importers will likely stay away

insights.claim: Major US importers are unlikely to touch Russian diesel because of contested legality (civil and criminal penalties with long statutes of limitations), bipartisan congressional scrutiny and reputational risk such as CEOs being called before Congress.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
insights.so_what: Expect no meaningful Russian diesel inflows to the US from mainstream commercial players, so no direct domestic price relief.

insights.claim: If imports occur at all, the likelier buyers are a government or government-adjacent entity or a small company close to Trump, not run-of-the-mill commercial actors; the SPR is a poor fit because it holds crude not diesel.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
insights.so_what: Watch for unusual buyers or government procurement as the only realistic US channel.

insights.claim: Trump's messaging shifted from importing Russian diesel into the US to putting it on global markets, and his Truth Social posts always said 'US and global markets' without committing to US arrivals, which suggests the administration recognizes commercial actors will not step up.
insights.speaker: Scott (host)
insights.so_what: Lowers the odds of US-bound cargoes and the domestic fuel price narrative.

insights.claim: Litigation is unlikely: it needs actual imports and a plaintiff with standing, such as a domestic refiner, biodiesel or renewable diesel producer or a Northeast distributor, and major energy firms are unlikely to fight the administration; the most plausible suit is an APA challenge to the license that could seek an injunction but not damages.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
insights.so_what: Legal risk is likely to show up as a future-enforcement overhang rather than near-term court rulings.

insights.claim: The authorized volume of about 4.8 million barrels is under 2% of US consumption over the period and a far smaller share of the global diesel market, so the price effect is expected to be small.
insights.speaker: Scott (host)
insights.so_what: Do not expect this license alone to move diesel prices.

insights.claim: Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries have cut Russian diesel exports from roughly 800,000 barrels per day last year to about 150,000, and Russia has restricted diesel exports under its own law, which is a bigger driver of global diesel prices than sanctions.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
insights.so_what: Refinery outages, not sanctions, are the key supply variable; ceasefire or repair news matters more for diesel cracks.

insights.claim: Rebuilding Russian refining capacity would take months, so meaningful additional export volume is unlikely within the six-month window even if strikes stop.
insights.speaker: Scott (host)
insights.so_what: Limits upside to Russian diesel supply near term.

insights.claim: Harrell and Alpert expect buyers outside the US, with India the leading candidate and possibly China, since the license gives non-US importers comfort to buy Russian diesel.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
insights.so_what: Watch Indian and Chinese import flows of Russian diesel as the real test of the license.

insights.claim: Past administrations also balanced sanctions against energy prices (Biden's price cap scheme kept Russian oil flowing, Obama phased Iranian oil reductions with partners), but those were multilateral, unlike this largely unilateral or bilateral move, which makes it less effective.
insights.speaker: Rachel Alpert
insights.so_what: Multilateral coordination is the differentiator for whether sanction easing affects prices.

insights.claim: Harrell speculates Trump may see the diesel license as pressure on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian refineries, while Alpert reads it the opposite way, as Putin getting the US to pressure Ukraine by persuading Trump that Ukrainian strikes drive high energy prices, his main political liability.
insights.speaker: Rachel Alpert
insights.so_what: US pressure on Ukraine over energy-infrastructure strikes can sustain Russian refining and export capacity.

insights.claim: Trump has declared an 'energy ceasefire' on Russian energy infrastructure without observable evidence one exists, and the US reportedly pushed Ukraine to limit refinery strikes since around September.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
insights.so_what: Track whether Ukrainian refinery strikes actually decline.

insights.claim: The deal appears tied to the midterms a few weeks away, raising the question of how long the position lasts afterward.
insights.speaker: Rachel Alpert
insights.so_what: Policy could reverse after the midterms.

themes.theme: Graham sanctions act and what to watch

insights.claim: The Graham sanctions law signed September 18 has its key tariff provision taking effect October 18, mandating tariffs greater than zero and up to 100% on major importers of Russian crude, with a broad national interest waiver; its crude definition excludes diesel (HTS 2709 vs 2710), so there is no hard legal conflict with GL 135.
insights.speaker: Scott (host)
insights.so_what: The October 18 implementation is a near-term catalyst for buyers of Russian crude, especially Indian and Chinese refiners.

insights.claim: Alpert would not be surprised if the broad waiver is used to justify non-action on tariffs on October 18, citing the diesel general license and bilateral trade negotiations.
insights.speaker: Rachel Alpert
insights.so_what: Base case is weak enforcement of the secondary tariff provision.

insights.claim: Harrell half-jokingly said Trump could be comfortable terrifying foreign buyers of Russian diesel while lowering US barriers, to funnel supply to the US and maximize domestic price reduction.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell
insights.so_what: Illustrates the inconsistency between the diesel license and the secondary-tariff law.

insights.claim: Indicators to watch include whether the general license is revoked under scrutiny, who buys and ships the diesel (vessels, insurers, flag states), and the effect on Ukraine's military position.
insights.speaker: Rachel Alpert
insights.so_what: These variables will show whether the arrangement has real market impact.
